video_title: Trump’s Tariffs Backfired Again. This Time in Brazil.
transcript: Lula lost the first round of [music] elections to Flavio and trailed in the polls for most of the race. >> No one expected this result and he ended up winning by 3.5 points. That's 4 million votes. Today's property plus deep dive is on the biggest election you probably didn't follow, Brazil, where voters just reelected their president Lula to a historic fourth term. Lula, a veteran of the left who first took office in 2003, beat Flavio Bolsonaro, the right-wing senator and son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, 51.8% to 48.2. He's now the first four-term president in Brazil's history. He's also the first candidate to lose the first round and come back to win the runoff since Brazil reinstated direct elections in 1989. The result surprised almost everyone. For most of the three weeks before the runoff, the polls had Flavio in front by as much as six points. The outcome also defied a broader regional shift. Since Trump returned to office, Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, and Honduras have all moved to the right. The biggest country in Latin America, Brazil, went the other way. Lula's win comes with a catch, however. Voters also elected the most conservative Congress since Brazil's return to democracy and Bolsonaro's party and its allies are set to control both chambers. Lula will be governing against that Congress with an economy under real strain. Brazil has one of the highest real interest rates on the planet, more than 9% after inflation. That's higher than Russia's, a country at war, and four times what peers including Chile and South Africa pay. In the US, it's close to zero. Even so, inflation is running at 4.6% above the central bank's tolerance range. A record of nearly 85 million Brazilians are behind on their debt payments and public debt has surged more than 10 points during Lula's current term to over 82% of GDP. Why should we care? Brazil is the largest economy in Latin America and the fourth largest democracy on Earth. And Donald Trump had a candidate in the race. Last year, he hit Brazil with 50% tariffs, at the time the highest he'd imposed on any country, and tied them directly to the prosecution of Jair Bolsonaro, who's now serving 27 years in prison for plotting to overturn the 2022 election. Flavio promised his father amnesty. If that sounds familiar or could be increasingly familiar, trust your instincts. Trump's tariffs on Canada helped hand Mark Carney a victory, and in Brazil, they helped turn a weakened incumbent into a nationalist hero. To unpack what comes next, our associate producer Laura Janaire, a Brazilian herself, sat down with Brian Winter, editor-in-chief of Americas Quarterly and vice president of policy at the Americas Society and Council of the Americas. Brian spent a decade reporting from Brazil, Argentina, and Mexico for Reuters. Here's Laura in conversation with Brian. >> Brian, [music] it's great to have you with us today. Thank you so much for doing this. >> It's a pleasure to be here. >> I'm currently in São Paulo, where we just lived through a historic election. Incumbent and left-wing president Lula won a fourth term, beating right-winger Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, and it was a pretty stunning comeback. Lula lost the first round of elections to Flavio and trailed in the polls for most of the race. No candidate had ever done that and still won the presidency since Brazil returned to direct elections in 1989. Investors also had priced in a Flavio win as well. Um but for anyone who doesn't follow Brazil closely, it's the fifth largest country in the world by area and the seventh by population with more than 213 million people. It's Latin America's largest economy and by the IMF's latest count, the 10th largest economy in the world, on track to pass Italy and Russia next year. It's also the fourth largest democracy on Earth. And if you drank coffee this morning, there's a good chance some of it came from here. Brazil is the world's biggest coffee exporter and supplies about a third of what Americans drink. Um but we'll get into how Lula pulled off the win and what it means for Brazil. But first, Brian, for people who don't follow Brazilian politics, why is this an election they should have been watching? >> Well, that's a great question. And you mentioned coffee. I've had a lot of it over the last several days in the wake of this election result, which as you mentioned, nobody saw coming. Uh you know, I speak to people on both sides of the political debate in Brazil, on left and on right. And in the Lula camp, no one expected this result. Because he lost by two percentage points in the first round. And their best hope was that maybe he just barely eke out a victory in the runoff. And he ended up winning by 3.5 percentage points. That's 4 million votes. To the question of why people should care about Brazil, couple basic things. The United States and Brazil are the two largest democracies in the Western Hemisphere. It's also the home to 2/3 of the Amazon rainforest, which is critical to the present and future of the planet. And there's also, you know, these bizarre parallels that we've seen between the United States and Brazil over the last 10 years or so. Ironic in a way because I spent the first half of my career telling US audiences, "Hey look, guys. Like Brazil is its own country. It has its own history, its own energy. Let's not be so self-obsessed and self-regarding to think that what happens in the United States will have an impact on the politics of Brazil." But there've been so many parallels really since the election of Donald Trump in 2016 and then the election of Jair Bolsonaro two years later. So, I think there's a lot that our countries have in common as well. So, when it comes to why we should care, I would start with those things. >> I'd love to come back to the parallels because as you said, there are definitely many Um especially with the recent Biden and and Trump election. But just to get back to the win, Lula's win. So he went from trailing to winning in like a pretty shocking 3 weeks. As we said, he gained roughly 10 million votes between the rounds compared to like 3.6 million for Flavio mostly through like higher turnout and picking up voters from eliminated candidates. And as the sitting president, Lula also made some big policy moves in that window. Um Congress passed a constitutional amendment ending Brazil's 6-day work week guaranteeing workers 2 days off with no pay cuts. For context, the 5-day work week is pretty standard in most developed economies. And Lula also raised Bolsa Familia, which is Brazil's main welfare program he himself started a couple decades ago um with bigger payments starting 6 days before the vote. And he also cut federal taxes on gasoline and launched a new debt relief program. But I'd love to ask you, what do you think really made the difference in those 3 weeks? Just so we can add some color to the sort of surprising turnaround. And one last follow up is the the US midterms are as this is released this week. So is there anything in how Lula turned this around that the that American campaigns on either side should also kind of pay attention to? What do you think of the the 3 weeks between the first and second round? >> Well Laura, as you mentioned, there were a variety of things that happened including this big bill that he ran up of more than 40 billion dollars worth of tax breaks and extra spending on welfare programs and so on. And that's part of the reason why financial markets were uh upset that Lula won. They had been counting on a Flavio Bolsonaro victory. But they, along with the rest of us, were wrong. And I have to say that these have been humbling days for me because I certainly Yeah, we we all sensed that the momentum was shifting in Lula's direction. But none of us expected it would swing quite this much. And I do wonder if there are lessons for Democrats in the United States or or perhaps anyone anybody anywhere looking to run a campaign in 2026 where you know the technological landscape has changed so much. And I would start with this basic fact. Lula at the age of 80 acquired his first smartphone in the final 2 weeks of the campaign. And you know part of your audience may think whoa. Why didn't he have one before? And that's a good question. You [clears throat] know he was an old school politician. Really a man of the 20th century. That was when he had his political rise was during the 1970s and the 1980s. But this is also a story of a modern digital operation that came out of nowhere in the space of 3 weeks between the first round of voting which Lula lost by two points and the second round which of course he ultimately won. And the stories that are coming out suggest that Lula was prevailed upon to allow a small group of young aides to go crazy. >> [laughter] >> You know online and specifically on WhatsApp. >> Yeah. >> Which is such a huge platform in Brazil along with others like Instagram and TikTok. I think it's important to pause here and note that there are various studies that show that Brazil is one of the countries in the world with the highest rate of engagement with social media. According to one study on average more than 6 hours a day and that includes WhatsApp as well as other platforms. And so this was perhaps a country that was especially ripe for this kind of campaign. So what happened? There was this young this one young congressman named Andre Janones. >> Yeah. >> Uh very close to Lula. Uh but who had been kept somewhat at arms length during the first round. And uh they liberated him, so to speak, to build out a digital army uh in the hopes of staging a comeback. And that's exactly what he did. He took a group uh that he had of some 50,000 people and just started He renamed it Lula's army. >> Mhm. >> And he just started building it out with constant content that, you know, it was an interesting dynamic because the foot soldiers in the army, so to speak, were allowed to post. It was It was all him and a couple of other people. >> Yeah. >> And they were given orders to post things online and so on. By the end of the campaign, this group had 10 million people. >> Wow. >> And uh if you had to point to one thing that turned Lula's campaign around, it was that. And of course, look, I mean, the campaign would have never worked had there not been actual content and ideas >> Sure. >> to use those channels for. But I can confirm for you, I've had conversations with people all over Latin America, including politicians, over the last couple days since this election result, and this is what they're all asking about, seeking to replicate for themselves. Because prior to that, it had really only been the right in Brazil that seemed to know how to use social media. This is something that, you know, progressive groups all over the world have struggled to match the engagement that the right has been able to muster. So, perhaps this really will turn into a case study that others around the world will will look at. >> But to that point, I'd love to ask you, how much do you think this win we can credit to Lula himself um versus it like how much do you think he was simply riding like an anti-Bolsonaro wave? And for some context, there's like high rejection to the Bolsonaro name in Brazil because of their association with an attempted coup in 2022, for which Jair Bolsonaro is currently serving 27 years. Again, Jair Bolsonaro is Flavio Bolsonaro's father. Since the Bolsonaro name is pretty tainted at this point, and and that even the choice to put Flavio Bolsonaro forward as the candidate that would, you know, represent sort of the right in Brazil is people see it as a mistake because there's a lot of voters in Brazil who see the presidential vote as a lesser of two evils, like who's least bad. Is it Lula or is it Bolsonaro? And using Bolsonaro against Lula might lead a lot a lot more people who aren't necessarily pro-Lula to vote for Lula because they're so scared of the Bolsonaro name as, you know, they have the sort of threat to democracy staying attached to to the their reputation because of Jair's um involvement with the coup. The Lula name is being floated as, you know, such an epic story in Brazilian politics, which is definitely true. But he is he's actually turning 81 today. It's his birthday today. You know, what elected him this time around? Do you think it was really um do you think you can credit his sort of cult of personality, or was it really just more of like a we're scared of Bolsonaro? >> I'm not sure Lula himself knows the answer to that question >> Yeah. >> as we sit here today. This is what everyone's trying to figure out. I mean, look, there there are philosophical questions in that you've raised about why people vote the way they do. Do they go into the ballot box thinking, "Oh gosh, I'm so happy to cast a vote for this candidate?" Or do they fear or hate >> Yeah. >> the person who they feel like they're casting a vote against? Many political scientists who have tried to understand this question in Brazil think it's the latter, that especially in a second-round runoff like the Brazilian system has, that it's usually about opposition to yes, people who want to avoid somebody coming back into power. But look, I think that some of this is inevitably wrapped up with Lula's story as well. And this is where, you know, the Brazilian case probably is not replicable elsewhere because there's nobody else in Latin American politics quite like Lula. If he completes this fourth term to which he's been elected, and I think it's fair to raise that given that he would be 85 by the time it's over, he will have been the main figure of Brazilian politics for an entire half century, for 50 years, dating from the 1979 strike in which he was a labor union leader under dictatorship who very bravely took a stand in favor of better working conditions for metal workers and others in Brazil at a time when when strikes were illegal. >> Yeah. >> And since that moment, you know, he ran for president for the first time in 1989, and he actually lost three elections before he won one. He finally won in 2002. This long career was one of Lula's weaknesses during the campaign. >> Yeah. >> For a US equivalent, lots of people compare Lula to Joe Biden. >> Yeah. >> And that makes sense because Lula was about the same age Biden was during his campaign. We all know how that ended. And I have to say that Lula uh has not shown, as at least as far as I've seen, any of the visible signs of physical or mental decline that the former president Biden did. But, I actually think that the proper analogy would be with Bill Clinton because Bill Clinton was elected for the first time in 1992. And we think about how long ago that was in our politics. Well, imagine if Bill Clinton had run in four elections since then. And that's roughly how Brazilians see Lula. But, look, you have to give the guy credit. He was able to put together one last winning campaign. I think a lot of it was centered around his biography and the connection that he has with Brazil's working classes because he is one of them. He's somebody who grew up, uh, you know, under very precarious circumstances, who sold oranges and cashews on the streets of São Paulo when his family moved there from northeastern Brazil, yeah, a very drought-stricken, poorer part of Brazil when he was just a kid. Like this was what people were really watching and reacting to. You know, the bottom line is don't blink >> [laughter] >> because the focus of a campaign and the narrative of a campaign in the age of smartphones and the age of social media can change so fast. I mean, I don't know that I've ever seen momentum change as dramatically, as quickly, as I did in this Brazilian race. And I don't think that was just because it was Brazil. I think [snorts] this has to do with um you know, with the way politics are now. When I visited Brazil on several occasions in 2026, I was struck by how hard it was to find anyone who was excited about either candidate. And so I think that was a dynamic where, you know, you had people who were declaring who they wanted to vote for to pollsters and others, but they weren't as sure as we thought they were. >> Mhm. >> And so, you know, maybe that's maybe that's another broader lesson as well. >> Totally. I'd love to come back to the US parallels. It'll start with one that I'll pose, which is the vibe session, a term that's kind of used in in the US. And the Financial Times had a recent article about this, where they described it as the Uberization of Brazil. So, I mean, the low unemployment number, at least we can't take it face value. And for a generation of Brazilians, this was their maximum aspiration. Not only did it mean a certain economic prosperity, or at least safety, um but it was also a source of prestige and pride in a lot of segments of the working class to have that kind of job. Well, today, not only have a lot of those jobs disappeared because of competition mainly from China. Um, but also uh, Brazilians in polls say that they would rather work for themselves. And that is a big change in the span of about 10 years. Like oh this is you know here's a gringo who's trying to to you know, to sound nice and sound complimentary. But I'll tell you, I speak to audiences all over the world about Brazil and about Latin America, and the further afield you travel, the more you're likely to see people nodding. These challenges that Lula faces with getting not only the government's debts, but household debts under control. In part because they've run up credit cards, but also in part because they've engaged in these betting apps, which have been so prominent over the last couple years. Uh he's going to have Lula's also going to have to deal with a congress that is much, much, much, much more conservative than he is. So, you spent a decade reporting from Brazil, Argentina, Mexico, and you've written about what you call Latin America's revolution of the rights. Um since Trump returned to office, Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, and Honduras have all shifted right or either shifted right or doubled down on a conservative turn. And over the past decade, governing parties across the region have lost election after election. Um but Lula managed to cut through both trends, both as a leftist leader and as incumbent. I think he, In doing so, he has escaped prison, but possibly ceded leadership for the entire Bolsonaro family >> Yeah. >> of the right-wing movement in Brazil. Any kind of progressive social agenda Lula, somewhat to the frustration of people on the left Lula has backed away from most of those issues over the last couple years. He was under pressure to from some quarters to try to support abortion rights, for example. He didn't want to touch that issue. >> Mhm. >> In part because polling shows 70% maybe more of Brazilians are against it. >> Mhm. >> Lula also one other example from the campaign. He late in the campaign decided that he would support efforts to lower the age of criminal responsibility in Brazil, meaning the age for which you can be sent to prison, tried as an adult, as we'd say here in the United States >> Yeah. >> from 18 to 16. This was something that his party had resisted for years and years. >> Mhm. >> And he finally acquiesced because he saw a need to tack right >> Yeah. >> especially on security issues during this campaign. So, while it's true that the right did not win per se in this Brazilian election, their influence was still very much felt. And part of Lula's success will be determined by whether he continues to recognize that today's Brazil really is in many ways a right-of-center country, even though they've just reelected a leftist president. >> Yeah. Um I don't know if you heard of that book um O Brasileiro Espelho, Brazilian the Mirror, where there's a big research done that found that actually the average Brazilian citizen is is kind of conservative and and right-wing, right? I think that was the takeaway from the book, which I was very surprised about cuz it's Lula's been in power for so long, you kind of forget that it's not necessarily reflective of and Brazil is also a huge country, which most people forget about, too. It's just so diverse demographically, also, and geographically, it's very hard to pin down just one simple description. Brian Winter is the editor-in-chief of Americas Quarterly and vice president of policy at the America Society and Council of the Americas. Brian, thank you so much for joining us. >> It was a real pleasure. I enjoyed it, too. Thank you.
